blocks.text: There are those who deny that bees hear. Yet on Es. VII, 18. The Lord shall hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria, Cyril writes thus: Πεποίηται τοίνυν ὁ λόγος, ὡς ἐκ μεταφορᾶς τῆς τῶν μελισσοκόμων ἐμπειρίας, οἳ συρίσμασι τὰς μυίας ἀποφέρον τί τε (read ἀποφέρουσί τε) τῶν σίμβλων εἰς ἀγροὺς, καὶ πάλιν ἀνακομίζουσι· [Pepoiētai toinyn ho logos, hōs ek metaphoras tēs tōn melissokomōn empeirias, hoi syrismasi tas myias apopheron ti te (read apopherousi te) tōn simblōn eis agrous, kai palin anakomizousi] The speech is figurative, a metaphor taken, as it were, from the skill of beekeepers, who by hissing call the flies out of the hives into the fields and lead them back again. And on Esa. V, 26. He will hiss for them from the end of the earth, the same Cyril writes: Δέχεται δὲ καὶ τοῦτο πάλιν, ὡς ἀπό γε τῆς συνηθείας τῆς ἐπὶ τῶν μυιῶν. Ἐν ἔθει γάρ πώς ἐστι τοῖς μελισσοκόμοις συρίζειν αὐταῖς· οὕτω τε τῶν σίμβλων ἀποφέρειν εἰς ἄνθη, καὶ πόας, καὶ μὴν καὶ ἀνακομίζειν ἐξ ἀγρῶν, οἴκοί τε αὐτὰς ἐναυλίζεσθαι ποιεῖν. [Dechetai de kai touto palin, hōs apo ge tēs synētheias tēs epi tōn myiōn. En ethei gar pōs esti tois melissokomois syrizein autais; houtō te tōn simblōn apopherein eis anthē, kai poas, kai mēn kai anakomizein ex agrōn, oikoi te autas enaulizesthai poiein.] He takes this again as if from the habit of flies (that is, of bees). For beekeepers are accustomed to hiss at them, and so to lead them out of the hives to flowers and herbs, and to call them back from the fields, and to make them stay at home. Others use the ringing of brass, or potsherds struck together, for the same purpose. Columella, book 9, ch. 8, §10: If (the swarm) is hidden in a cave, it will be drawn out with smoke; and when it has burst out, it is checked by the clashing of brass. And ch. 12: Let the fleeing young swarm be frightened with brass rattles, or with the sound of potsherds, which usually lie about everywhere. Pliny, book 11, ch. 20: They delight in clapping and the ringing of brass, and are called together by it. From which it is clear that they also have the sense of hearing. Aelian, book 5, ch. 13: Ὅταν γοῦν σκιρτήσωσιν, καὶ πλανηθῶσιν, ἐνταῦθα οἱ σμηνουργοὶ κροτοῦσι [III, 359] κρότον τινὰ ἐμμελῆ τε, καὶ συμμελῆ. αἱ δὲ ὡς ὑπὸ σειρῆνος ἕλκονται, καὶ μέντοι ὑποστρέφουσιν εἰς τὰ οἰκεῖα αὖθις. [Hotan goun skirtēsōsin, kai planēthōsin, entautha hoi smēnourgoi krotousi kroton tina emmelē te, kai symmelē. hai de hōs hypo seirēnos helkontai, kai mentoi hypostrephousin eis ta oikeia authis.] When they frolic and stray, the beekeepers then make a melodious and harmonious sound. And they are drawn back as if by a Siren, and return to their accustomed homes. Virgil:
Raise a ringing, and shake the cymbals of Mars around;
that is, so that you may call the wandering bees back to the hives. And a little later, when they go out to battle:
— — — — — the laggards that Martial blare of hoarse brass rebukes, and a voice is heard imitating the broken blasts of trumpets.
Following the sound of the Curetes and the clashing brass, they fed the king of heaven beneath the Dictaean cave.

And now they had come to Rhodope and the Pangaean streams, when the brass-bearing hands of his companions clashed. Behold! new winged creatures gather, driven by the ringing, and the bees follow the brass whose sounds they hear.
— — as when the sound of Phrygian brass rings out, astonished, they cease their flight, and return to their eager flower-gathering labour and the love of sacred honey.
Claudian, Panegyric on the sixth Consulship of Honorius, line 259: [col. 507]
— — — as the old Hyblaean man, shaking from afar the Cybelean brass, tries with the ringing to recall the fugitive bees, which of their own accord have deserted and left their honeycombs. — — — —
